title: How many pieces with six points?
hook: Points on a circle, every pair joined: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 pieces. What comes next?

doesNotKnow: that a pattern holding for five cases can still break, and why this one does (pieces = 1 + lines + crossings)

misconception: 2, 4, 8, 16 must continue as 32: a pattern that held five times is proved.
objective: The learner can say that 6 points on a circle give 31 pieces, not 32, because pieces = 1 + lines + crossings (1 + 15 + 15), and that five matching cases are evidence, not a proof.

claims.text: With the stage's points (at 0°, 64°, 113°, 179°, 230°, 308°, the first n for n points), every pair joined, the circle is cut into 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31 pieces for 1 to 6 points, with 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 lines and 0, 0, 0, 1, 5, 15 crossings: doubling held up to 5 points and broke at 6, so five matching cases are evidence, not a proof. Recall: a rule that holds in the first five cases you try can still fail in a later one.
claims.source: company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label D3 (crossings 0, 0, 0, 1, 5, 15; regions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31 by Euler's formula on the drawing; formula 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4) agrees). Stage: drawingOf() in Demo.tsx counts crossings by segment intersection and pieces by Euler's formula (E − V + 1), not by the formula.
claims.note: v2 recheck: ANGLES unchanged; recomputed lines 0,1,3,6,10,15, crossings 0,0,0,1,5,15 (all distinct, min separation 0.209 R), pieces 1,2,4,8,16,31. Agrees with D3.

claims.text: When no three lines meet at one point, pieces = 1 + lines + crossings = 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4): every piece is made by a line or a crossing (each line, drawn in turn, adds 1 piece plus 1 for each crossing it makes), so with 6 points it is 1 + 15 + 15 = 31 and the rule was never doubling: it only matched doubling up to 5 points.
claims.source: Adding a chord that crosses k earlier chords at distinct points splits k + 1 pieces, so pieces = 1 + chords + crossings; chords = C(n,2) (claim c3), crossings = C(n,4) (claim c3). Agrees with D3 for n = 1 to 6.
claims.note: v2 recheck: the formula 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4) under no-three-concurrent is right, and so is 1 + 15 + 15 = 31. The reworded clause "the rule was never doubling: it only matched doubling up to 5 points" is true (1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4) = 1,2,4,8,16 then 31,57).

claims.text: Lines come from pairs of points, C(n,2) of them, and crossings from groups of four: each set of four points on the circle gives exactly one crossing (its two diagonals), so there are C(n,4) crossings when no three lines meet at one point.
claims.source: Four points on a circle form a convex quadrilateral whose two diagonals cross once inside and whose sides do not cross; two chords cross inside the circle only if their four end points alternate around it, i.e. they are the diagonals of that quadrilateral. D3: crossings 1, 5, 15 = C(4,4), C(5,4), C(6,4).
claims.note: v2 recheck: two chords cross inside exactly when their end points alternate, so each 4-set gives one crossing; C(n,4) = 1, 5, 15 recomputed.

claims.text: With 6 evenly spaced points there are 30 pieces, because three diagonals meet at the centre; this is why the predict question states that the points are uneven so no three lines meet at one spot (meta evidence; the learner sees only the condition).
claims.source: company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label D3, regular hexagon: 15 crossings, 13 distinct points, max 3 lines through one point, 30 regions.
claims.note: v2 recheck: regular hexagon has 15 crossing pairs on 13 distinct points (3 long diagonals at the centre), so 30 pieces. Agrees with D3.

recall.question: You test a rule on the first five cases you try and it works every time. What have you shown?
options: It is evidence, but a later case could still break it
The sixth case must break it
recall.why: The circle pieces doubled five times and then gave 31, not 32: matching cases are evidence, and only a reason why the rule holds proves it.
